html:
Onimusha has always been an interesting anomaly in Capcom’s library of franchises. Originally conceived in 1997 as a Resident Evil game set in feudal Japan, the first entry in the samurai action adventure series was released early in the PlayStation 2’s life cycle. And while it may have seemed like the furthest thing from a traditional Resident Evil title, Onimusha featured many of the horror game's hallmarks, including a focus on puzzles, fixed camera angles, and tank controls. Now, more than 20 years since the last entry in the series, Onimusha: Way of the Sword ($69.99, tested on PlayStation 5 Pro and Nintendo Switch 2, available on PC, Xbox Series X, and Xbox Series S) is tasked with both reintroducing the long-dormant series while simultaneously modernizing its action-adventure gameplay.

Is it perfect? No. But does it succeed at reintroducing and revitalizing an obscure franchise for the masses? Yes, it does.

Welcome Back, Onimusha

I’ve been eager to play Onimusha: Way of the Sword since I first saw it behind closed doors at Summer Game Fest 2025. To me, a great measure of a developer's or publisher's success is whether they’re willing to invest in a game that might be considered a business risk. Onimusha games, despite having many fans, are not exactly on the same tier as mega hits like Monster Hunter, Street Fighter, or Resident Evil. But Capcom has been on such a hot streak lately that it's heartening to see them take a stab (pun intended) at a new entry.

Way of the Sword, like pretty much every game released by Capcom since 2017’s Resident Evil 7, is powered by Capcom’s in-house RE engine. But this is probably Capcom’s most visually impressive game to date—and that’s saying a lot considering Capcom released Resident Evil Requiem, Pragmata, and Monster Hunter Stories 3 this year alone. But what I found most striking about the game is the facial animation in cutscenes. Using the likeness of late actor Toshiro Mifune certainly helps, but there’s a lot of subtle and not-so-subtle facial work in this game that breathes life into Miyamoto Musashi, the titular Onimusha.

Preorder Onimusha: Way of the Sword

Onimusha: Way of the Sword


Although it’s not the first time Capcom has used an actor's likeness in an Onimusha game (and, most surprisingly, not the first time they’ve used a dead actor’s likeness), the use of Toshiro Mifune gives Way of the Sword a certain level of prestige not seen in previous entries. A name that film buffs will likely recognize, Mifune was largely associated with the works of equally legendary director Akira Kurosawa. Together, they made 16 movies together, including Seven Samurai, Sanjuro, and Yojimbo.

Many of Mifune's films cast him in hypermasculine roles, though Mifune’s performances were often layered. He could be threatening, heroic, and, at times, goofy. In Kurosawa’s memoir, Something of an Autobiography, he wrote, “The ordinary Japanese actor might need ten feet of film to get across an impression; Mifune needed only three. The speed of his movements was such that he said in a single action what took ordinary actors three separate movements to express.”

(Credit: Capcom)

One of the game’s opening cutscenes channels all three of these qualities. As Musashi scrambles through a school of Samurai, the game seamlessly bounces between skillful swordplay, rowdy improvisation, and Looney Tunes-style levity. At one point, Musashi slips on mud and slides headfirst through a crowd of Samurai. They all stop and stare for a beat, as if to ask: “Did he mean to do that?” Judging from the yelp Musashi lets out when his head collides with the wall, I don’t think he did.

It’s one thing to nail that type of performance in pre-rendered cutscenes, but it's another entirely to tie that feeling to gameplay, and I think Way of the Sword nails this well. In the twenty years since Onimusha has been gone, Soulslike games have become the norm for action titles, and Way of the Sword is no different. 

Incredible Combat

But unlike FromSoftware’s titles, Musashi’s movements don’t feel as clunky or heavy; in fact, they're more in line with recent titles like Lies of P and Stellar Blade. There’s an elegance to the swordplay that becomes especially clear once you start to master parrying and dodging your opponents. It won’t take long before you find yourself surrounded by enemies, bouncing between them as you clash swords, reflect projectiles, and even push enemies into one another. After every clash, Musashi collects the departed souls of his enemies, which act has both the game’s currency and resource for replenishing health and your special attack meter.

(Credit: Capcom)

It’s a far cry from the clunky swordplay of those original games. While some detractors may say that these modern gameplay stylings diminish Onimusha’s originality (a criticism I’ve seen launched at recent remakes like Silent Hill 2 and Resident Evil 2), I’d say that Onimusha iterates on this action formula enough to feel fresh and satisfying. For example, Way of the Sword rewards defensive play in the form of Issen, powerful counterattacks that are triggered by attacking before an enemy strikes. These deal heavy damage, and if you're fighting against weaker foes, you can chain your Issen's together, cutting down waves of enemies in fast bursts. Clashing swords can also lead to a quick QTE guessing game. Choose the right button and cut through your enemy. Choose the wrong one and get cut through.

While clearing mobs of enemies can be fun, the combat really shines during the game’s many boss fights. These battles, usually against Oni from Japanese folklore, provide the game’s most exciting—and challenging—moments. The boss fights felt larger than life, and while I did come close to chucking my controller a few times, most of the boss fights felt fair, rewarding patience and defensive play.

But even if you’re lacking in patience or skill, new accessibility options like button prompts and difficulty options will certainly help players improve their timing and get past difficulty fights that would otherwise stop play. These can be switched on or off at any time, without penalty.

Some Kinks in the Armor

The game is split between linear areas that feel most like older Onimusha games and Eastern Kyoto, which resembles a more traditional open world that acts as a hub for Musashi. The game is split between both areas, though players can use the Spirit Mirrors to traverse between them. Most of the game takes place in Eastern Kyoto, though the lives of its citizens have been made worse by the invading Genma, monster-like samurai who know only violence, and an encroaching miasma of malice that poisons everything it touches. As Musashi clears away the malice, the locals come out of hiding, and more of Kyoto becomes available to explore.

Eastern Kyoto reminded me of games like Like a Dragon/Yakuza games, particularly Like A Dragon: Ishin! As the world expands, Musashi can go around taking on requests from the townfolk for resources to upgrade his sword, armor, and gauntlet. Unfortunately, these parts of the game don’t shine as brightly as the combat. The missions aren’t as silly or emotional as your average Yakuza side story, but they also all mostly require the same thing – traveling from point A to point B to slaughter something or someone. The exceptions are the Curious Case files, which are missions that expand on Kyoto Folklore. They’re not that much more involved, but they are at least more interesting.

(Credit: Capcom)

I almost wished there was more to do in Kyoto. There aren’t any side activities to participate in, and aside from some collectibles, there’s no real incentive to explore either. I don’t need Way of the Sword to be littered with mundane time wasters, but I wish there were more of a reason to take in the sights instead of just rushing to the nearest Spirit Mirror and fast traveling to your destination.

Luckily, if the open world mission structure isn’t exciting to you, you can train with Takamura, Musashi’s mentor and fellow Onimusha. Here you can practice techniques through drills and replay boss fights. This area reminded me of the Training Simulation in Pragmata, and because they still reward you with items and materials for upgrades, they’re well worth checking out.

But as much as I enjoyed Onimusha, the game does start to drag, especially toward the end. While sword play never dulls, you’ll find yourself chopping down miasma-spewing plants and absorbing rifts very often. Enemy variety is nothing to write home about either, with only a few types of enemies that, while growing stronger as you advance through the game, don’t really change up their fighting style much. There's also a serious lack of puzzles.

(Credit: Capcom)

Musashi also finds many Oni weapons on his journey, but they can only be used once before needing to be charged with blue souls. While they serve as good ways to deal damage to bosses or handle large groups of enemies, Musashi sticks to his sword and sword alone. I do think this is a missed opportunity to add some variety to the combat. Different weapons or even weapon styles could’ve added some variety to Onimusha’s combat.

But What About the Switch 2 Version?

While I played and completed Onimusha: Way of the Sword on a PlayStation 5 Pro, I was also able to spend time with the Switch 2 version, and it’s one of the most impressive games on the system. Capcom has proven itself to be one of the platform's biggest supporters, bringing nearly all of its new and old releases to the platform. Although there are some cutbacks in visual fidelity and performance, these games prove that the hybrid console is a more-than-capable platform for modern releases.

Now I don’t have frame rate software, but switching from the solid 60fps of the PlayStation to the uncapped frame rate of the Switch 2 (docked) wasn’t as big a drop as I expected. In fact, I thought the performance held up better than both Resident Evil Requiem and Pragmata did, because Onimusha didn’t have as many noticeable frame rate lurches like those games did, even in the open world segments in Eastern Kyoto, at least from my hour and a half with the Switch 2 version. There’s a 30fps lock available as well, but the uncapped frame rate felt so good that I didn’t feel the need to lock it.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword captured on Nintendo Switch 2 (Credit: Capcom)

This is even better in handheld mode, thanks to the screen's variable refresh rate (VRR) support. VRR is a display technology that dynamically matches your screen's refresh rate to the changing frame rates. So even if the Switch 2’s frame rate is unsteady, the handheld screen will hide the stutters and dips. While resolution does take a pretty big hit in handheld mode, it’s perfectly playable, and Way of the Sword’s muted color palette still preserves the picture pretty well. But most importantly, Playing Onimusha: Way of the Sword has left me confident in Capcom’s two most ambitious Switch 2 ports: Dragon’s Dogma 2 and Monster Hunter Wilds.

Final Thoughts

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is not as perfect as a Hatori Hanzo blade, but it’s still a lot of fun. The boss fights are incredible, the sword play is fast and fluid, and the visuals are outstanding on both high and low-end gear. While the lack of mission variety and a boring hub area are low lights in Onimusha’s revival, the overall package is one that is sure to impress the hell out of returning veterans of the series and newcomers looking for a satisfying samurai action game. The CapGods have done it again, proving they own 2026 with yet another excellent release.

Experience

I’m a PCMag reviewer and ISF-certified TV calibrator focused on computer accessories, laptops, gaming monitors, and video games. I’ve been writing, playing, and complaining about games for as long as I remember, but it wasn’t until recently that I’ve been able to shout my opinions directly at a larger audience. My work has appeared on iMore, Windows Central, Android Central, and TWICE, and I have a diverse portfolio of editing work under my belt from my time spent at Scholastic and Oxford University Press. I also have a few book-author credits under my belt—I’ve contributed to the sci-fi anthology Under New Suns, and I’ve even written a Peppa Pig book.
